passages.t: The first warning: do not drift away
passages.happening:
Now the writer turns from teaching to urging. If the Son is so great, then his word must be heard.

“We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away” (verse 1).

He gives his reason. “For if the message spoken by angels was binding, and every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment, how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” (verses 2-3).

Then he says where this salvation came from. It “was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him, and was affirmed by God through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will” (verses 3-4).
passages.hearers:
This is the first of the letter's five warnings. Notice the word ‘we’. The writer does not point at his readers from outside. He stands with them under the warning.

‘Drift away’ is a word used of a boat slipping past its harbour, or a ring slipping off a finger. The danger is not a sudden, angry turning away. It is slow and quiet. A person stops paying attention, and the current carries them off without their noticing.

The argument goes from the smaller to the greater, a common way of reasoning among Jewish teachers. ‘The message spoken by angels’ means the law given at Sinai. Exodus does not mention angels there, but many Jews believed that angels had a part in giving the law, and Stephen and Paul both say so (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19). That law was ‘binding’: it was God's word, and it was not to be ignored. If that word mattered so much, how much more the word spoken by the Lord himself?

Verse 3 tells us something about the writer. He did not hear Jesus himself. The message came to him from ‘those who heard Him’. So he and his readers belonged to the second generation of believers. And God had backed up the message with signs, wonders and gifts of the Spirit, as Acts tells.
passages.ot:
The law given at Sinai is the ‘message’ of verse 2. Moses' blessing pictures the LORD coming from Sinai “with myriads of holy ones” (Deuteronomy 33:2). The Greek Old Testament of that verse speaks of angels with God, and Jewish tradition built on it.

That law did carry penalties. Moses warned Israel that the covenant came with blessings and curses: “See, I have set before you today life and goodness, as well as death and disaster” (Deuteronomy 30:15).

The picture of drifting has an Old Testament echo too. The psalms call God's people to keep listening: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (Psalm 95:7-8). Hebrews will quote those words in the next chapter.

And ‘signs and wonders’ is the language of the exodus, when God showed his power in Egypt: “the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, with great terror, signs, and wonders” (Deuteronomy 26:8). The God who acted then has acted again in the gospel.
passages.hard:
‘How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?’ Can a believer drift so far that they are lost?

This is the first of the letter's warnings, and the same question runs through all five. Christians answer it in more than one way. Much of the Reformed and Baptist world holds that those truly saved are kept by God and cannot finally be lost. They read the warning as real and serious, one of the means God uses to keep his people: true believers hear it and pay attention. Much of the Wesleyan, Arminian and Catholic world holds that a person can turn away and forfeit salvation, and reads the warning more directly. These notes do not choose. The site's note on Romans 8:31-39 sets out both, and so does the Honest Answer, ‘Can you lose your salvation?’ The book page's part on the warning passages says more.

Both agree on what the warning is about: neglect, a slow letting go of Christ. It is not about having doubts, or feeling far from God for a time, or failing and coming back. The cure the writer gives is simple: pay attention to what you have heard.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Drifting is quiet. Ask whether there is a place in your life where you have stopped paying attention to what you heard about Jesus. Ask what pulls you, like a current, away from him. And ask what it would look like this week to ‘pay closer attention’: to read, to listen, to pray, to stay near other believers.

passages.happening:
The writer returns to the angels. “For it is not to angels that He has subjected the world to come, about which we are speaking” (verse 5).

He quotes a psalm about human beings: “What is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him? You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor and placed everything under his feet” (verses 6-8).

Then he looks around. “When God subjected all things to him, He left nothing outside of his control. Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him” (verse 8).

“But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, so that by the grace of God He might taste death for everyone” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
‘The world to come’ is the new world God is bringing, the world the Son will rule. It is not given to angels. It is given to human beings, as the psalm says.

‘But somewhere it is testified’ (verse 6) is not a sign that the writer forgot where the psalm was. He cares more about who speaks in Scripture than where. All through the letter he treats Scripture as God speaking.

The writer reads the psalm in two steps. First, the psalm says God made human beings to rule his world, with everything under their feet. But that is not what we see. People do not rule the world well. Death and sin seem to rule them. Second, what we do see is Jesus. He went down, ‘a little lower than the angels’, into a real human life and a real death. And now he is ‘crowned with glory and honor’. In him the psalm's picture of humanity has come true. He is the first of a new humanity.

‘Taste death’ means to experience death fully. It does not mean a small sip. And he did it ‘for everyone’, ‘by the grace of God’. His death was a gift.
passages.ot:
Verses 6 to 8 quote Psalm 8: “what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him? You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor. You made him ruler of the works of Your hands; You have placed everything under his feet” (Psalm 8:4-6).

In its own setting the psalm is a song of wonder. A man looks up at the night sky and feels tiny. Yet God has given human beings, frail as they are, a king's honour and a place to rule over the animals and the earth. It echoes Genesis 1, where God makes humankind “to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the livestock, and over all the earth itself” (Genesis 1:26). ‘Son of man’ in the psalm is a Hebrew way of saying ‘a human being’.

‘A little lower than the angels’ is how the Berean Standard Bible renders the psalm, but the Hebrew word there, elohim, most often means ‘God’. So some Bibles read ‘a little lower than God’, and others ‘than the heavenly beings’. The Greek Old Testament read ‘angels’, and Hebrews follows it, as the site's note on Psalm 8 explains. The difference comes from how to translate the word, not from a different text. Hebrews can also read ‘a little’ as ‘for a little while’, which fits its point: Jesus was lower for a time, and now is crowned.
passages.hard:
Who did Jesus die for, if he tasted death ‘for everyone’?

Christians agree that this verse does not teach that every person will be saved whatever they do; the same letter warns against neglecting salvation (verse 3). Beyond that, they differ, as they do on similar verses such as 1 John 2:2. Many, including Arminian and much of Lutheran and evangelical thought, read it as teaching that Christ died for every person without exception, a sacrifice enough for all and offered to all, received by faith. Those who hold to particular or definite atonement, common in Reformed theology, read ‘everyone’ in the light of the next verses, which speak of ‘many sons’, his ‘brothers’ and ‘the children God has given Me’ (verses 10-13): Christ died for all his people, from every nation. Some hold a middle view: his death is enough for all, and effective for those who believe. These notes do not choose.

What all agree on is what the verse says plainly: his death was ‘by the grace of God’, a gift, and its reach is wider than any one group.

A second question: does ‘a little lower than the angels’ mean the Son stopped being God? No. The church confesses that the Son, ‘very God of very God’, ‘came down from heaven’ and ‘was made man’. He took a lower place by becoming human. He did not stop being who he was.
passages.asks: We do not yet see everything put right. But we see Jesus. Ask where you are looking at what is wrong in the world, and in you, and losing heart. Then ask what it means to look at Jesus, who went down into death and is crowned. And ask what it means that the crown of a true human life was won by suffering, not by escaping it.

passages.t: Not ashamed to call them brothers
passages.happening:
“In bringing many sons to glory, it was fitting for God, for whom and through whom all things exist, to make the author of their salvation perfect through suffering” (verse 10).

Then the writer shows how close Jesus has come to his people. “For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers” (verse 11).

He gives three passages from Scripture, as words spoken by Jesus. “I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly” (verse 12). “I will put My trust in Him” (verse 13). And “Here am I, and the children God has given Me” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
‘Sons’ here means all God's children, men and women alike, who share in the inheritance. God is bringing them ‘to glory’, the full life of the world to come.

‘Author’ translates a Greek word that means a pioneer or champion, someone who goes first and opens a way for others to follow. Think of a leader who cuts a path through a forest so that a whole family can come after him. Jesus went through suffering and death and out the other side, and he leads his people after him.

‘The One who sanctifies’ is Jesus, who makes his people holy, set apart for God. ‘Those who are sanctified’ are his people. They are ‘of the same family’. In the ancient world, belonging to a family meant duties: a relative would pay a debt to free you from slavery, or stand up for you. Jesus takes those duties on himself.

And he is ‘not ashamed’ of them. The readers knew shame. They had been mocked in public for their faith (10:33). Their own society may have been ashamed of them. Jesus is not.
passages.ot:
Verse 12 quotes Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross. It begins in agony, “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1). But it ends in praise, as the sufferer is rescued and thanks God among his people: “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; I will praise You in the assembly” (Psalm 22:22). Hebrews hears the risen Jesus speaking these words, praising God among those he calls brothers.

Verse 13 quotes Isaiah 8. In a time of fear and war, the prophet Isaiah chose to trust God when others did not: “I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding His face from the house of Jacob. I will put my trust in Him” (Isaiah 8:17). Then he pointed to his own children, whose names were signs from God: “Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel” (Isaiah 8:18). In its setting it is about Isaiah and his family, a faithful few in a faithless time. Hebrews hears in it Jesus, who trusted God, and the children God has given him.

The idea of a relative who frees his family is an old one in Israel. The law spoke of a kinsman who could buy back a relative sold into slavery: “One of his brothers may redeem him” (Leviticus 25:48).
passages.hard:
‘Make the author of their salvation perfect through suffering’ (verse 10). Was Jesus once less than perfect?

No. The letter itself rules that out. Jesus was tempted ‘yet was without sin’ (4:15), and he is ‘holy, innocent, undefiled’ (7:26). In Hebrews, ‘perfect’ means complete, brought to the goal. In the Greek Old Testament the same family of words is used for setting a priest apart for his work. Jesus was ‘made perfect’ in that sense: by going all the way through obedience, suffering and death, he was made complete as the Saviour and high priest of his people. He did not become more God, or more good. He became, by living it, the fully tested human priest who knows our life from inside.

The church confesses Christ as one person, ‘truly God and truly man’, ‘in all things like unto us, without sin’, in the words of the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451. A real human life grows and learns. Luke says the boy Jesus “grew in wisdom and stature” (Luke 2:52). Christians hold that this belongs to his true humanity and takes nothing from his being God.

Why was it ‘fitting’ for God to do it this way? The writer does not explain it as a rule God had to keep. He says it suited who God is: the God for whom all things exist chose to bring his children home through a brother who shared their suffering.
passages.asks: Jesus is not ashamed to call his people brothers and sisters. Ask whether you believe that about yourself, in the places where you feel shame. Ask how you treat the other members of this family, the ones Jesus is not ashamed of. And ask where you need a pioneer who has gone ahead of you through suffering.

passages.t: He shared our flesh and blood
passages.happening:
“Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death” (verses 14-15).

“For surely it is not the angels He helps, but the descendants of Abraham” (verse 16).

“For this reason He had to be made like His brothers in every way, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God, in order to make atonement for the sins of the people. Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted” (verses 17-18).
passages.hearers:
‘Flesh and blood’ means human life, with a body that can be hurt and can die. The Son took that life. He did not only look human. He was human.

People in the ancient world lived with the fear of death. Many graves carried hopeless words, and teachers of philosophy wrote to help people stop fearing death. Hebrews says that fear is a kind of slavery, and that the devil uses it. Jesus broke that slavery from the inside, by dying and rising. He did not avoid death. He went through it and broke its hold.

‘The descendants of Abraham’ may mean Israel, or all who share Abraham's faith (Galatians 3:29). Either way, Jesus came to help God's people, not the angels. ‘Helps’ pictures taking someone by the hand to rescue them.

Here, for the first time, the letter calls Jesus ‘high priest’. Chapters 4 to 10 will explain it. A high priest stood between God and the people. He had to belong to the people, so he could speak for them. That is why the Son had to become ‘like His brothers in every way’. ‘Merciful’ means he feels for them. ‘Faithful’ means he can be trusted with God's work. And ‘make atonement’ means to deal with sin so that it no longer stands between God and people.
passages.ot:
The story behind verses 14 and 15 begins in Genesis 3, where death enters the world through the serpent's lie. God promised that the woman's offspring would strike back: “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (Genesis 3:15). Many Christians have read that promise as fulfilled in Christ's victory over the evil one.

The prophets hoped for the day death would be defeated: “He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face” (Isaiah 25:8). And “Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?” (Hosea 13:14).

‘Make atonement for the sins of the people’ is the language of Israel's high priest on the Day of Atonement, the one day each year he went into the Most Holy Place: Aaron went in “to make atonement in the Most Holy Place” for “himself, his household, and the whole assembly of Israel” (Leviticus 16:17).
passages.hard:
If Jesus destroyed the devil's power over death, why do people, believers included, still die and still fear death?

Hebrews speaks of a victory already won whose full result is still to come. Paul says the same: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26). Believers still die. What Christ has broken is death's power to hold them, and the slavery of a fear with no hope beyond it. All Christians confess that Jesus Christ truly died and was bodily raised, and that those who belong to him will be raised too.

These verses do not ask anyone to be calm about dying on demand. The Bible calls death an enemy, and Jesus wept at a grave (John 11:35). Fear of dying is human, and grief for someone who has died is love going on.

If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And ‘tempted’ in verse 18: Jesus was tempted, and the letter says he was without sin (4:15). Being tempted is not the same as sinning. If you are being tempted now, the one you pray to knows what it is like, and he is able to help.
passages.asks: Jesus became like us in every way so that he could help us. Ask what you are afraid of, and whether fear of death or loss is ruling you in quiet ways. Ask what it means to bring your temptations to someone who has felt their pull and did not give in. And ask what help you need from him today.
